claims.text: Increasing grain-boundary precipitate density reduces high-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing alloys.
Increasing grain-boundary precipitate density reduces high-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing alloys.
Grain-boundary precipitates impede dislocation mobility.
Dislocation obstruction by grain-boundary precipitates produces localized stress concentrations.
The localized stress concentrations caused by grain-boundary precipitates trigger early cavitation.
Early cavitation reduces the alloy's capacity to accommodate plastic strain.
Reduced plastic-strain accommodation diminishes toughness.
A modified thermal treatment and controlled cooling rate can increase precipitate density and alter precipitate distribution specifically along grain boundaries.
The range 1100–1400°C represents fusion-relevant high-temperature testing conditions for the proposed alloy.
Controlling cooling rate during testing or processing isolates precipitate density as the causal variable.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, the high-precipitate-density sample will have lower plastic strain than the low-density baseline.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, the high-precipitate-density sample will have lower fracture toughness than the low-density baseline.
The proposed relationship should hold from 1100°C to 1400°C for alloys of similar composition.
The effect may differ outside 1100–1400°C or in substantially different alloy chemistries.
The magnitude of the ductility and toughness changes may vary with alloy composition and microstructural details.
Threshold precipitate sizes and densities governing the proposed transition have not been established.
Two same-composition alloy sets subjected to modified versus standard thermal processing provide the proposed controlled comparison.
Grain-boundary precipitate density can be quantified by TEM or SEM imaging.
A lack of a statistically significant decrease in plastic strain and fracture toughness in the confirmed high-density samples would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between precipitate density and altered dislocation behavior would falsify the proposed mechanism.
